read.sections.0.heading.source: Why some languages have more writing
read.sections.0.heading.back: Why some languages have more writing

read.sections.0.text.source: AI tools that write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For them, it is a huge amount of writing, much of it from the internet. Most big AI tools learned mainly from English. How much writing a language has depends on history. Which languages do schools teach in? Which ones do people publish books and newspapers in? Which ones do governments use for laws and forms? And which ones do people type online? In Harbourside, schools and offices use Languages A and B, so little is written in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. They say that rule by other countries in the past did great harm to African languages. Technology still shows that harm.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI tools that can write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For these tools the training data is a huge amount of writing, much of it from the internet. Most large AI tools learn mainly from English. How much writing a language has depends on history. What language do schools teach in? What language do people publish books and newspapers in? What language does the government write laws and forms in? And what language do people type on the internet? In Harbourside, schools and offices use Language A and Language B, so there is very little writing in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. They say that other countries ruling in the past did great damage to African languages, and technology today still shows that damage.
read.sections.0.text.note: Masakhane's view of colonial rule: translated as การที่ประเทศอื่นเคยเข้ามาปกครองในอดีต ("other countries ruling in the past") to stay plain and close to the English; check it reads neutral and not softened. Reviewer: “much of it from the internet”: ส่วนใหญ่ (most) changed to จำนวนมาก (much).

In Harbourside, schools use Languages A and B. So little is written in Language C. Some African experts say the past matters too. Other countries once ruled much of Africa, and this hurt African languages.

read.sections.1.text.source: A low-resource language has little digital material that computers can use for a task. The name is about data, not about the language or its speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili. But Stanford researchers say there is not enough Swahili writing online for AI to learn well. In 2025, they found that big AI tools worked well in English. They worked less well in Vietnamese, and worse in Nahuatl, a language of Mexico. Less training data is one possible reason for a gap like this, but not the only one. How a tool is built and tested matters too. Translating from English doesn't fix it all. It can miss how people really speak.
read.sections.1.text.back: A low-resource language is a language with little digital content for computers to use for certain tasks. The name is about the data, not about the language itself or the people who speak it. About 200 million people speak Swahili, but Stanford researchers say there is still not enough Swahili writing on the internet for AI to learn well. In 2025 they found that large AI tools work well in English, less well in Vietnamese, and worse still in Nahuatl, a language of Mexico. Having less training data is one possible cause of a gap like this, but not the only one; how tools are built and tested matters too. Translating from English does not solve everything, because it may miss how people really speak.
read.sections.1.text.note: Language names written in Thai script (ภาษาสวาฮีลี, ภาษานาวาตล์); the checker warns that the Latin names Nahuatl, Sundanese, Batak, Bahasa and Patois are missing, which is expected. Check the transliteration นาวาตล์ for Nahuatl.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Some languages have little writing or speech for computers. We call this a low-resource language. The name is about data. It is not about the language or the people. Many millions of people speak Swahili. But there is not much written in it online. In 2025, researchers found big tools worked best in English. They worked less well in Vietnamese, and worse in Nahuatl. Less data is one reason for a gap. How a tool is built and tested matters too. To translate from English does not fix it all.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Some languages have little writing or speech for computers to use. We call such a language a low-resource language. The name is about data, not about the language or the people. Many millions of people speak Swahili, but there is not much writing in it on the internet. In 2025 researchers found that big tools work best in English, less well in Vietnamese, and worse in Nahuatl. Less data is one cause of this gap. How tools are built and tested matters too. Translating from English does not solve everything.

read.sections.2.text.source: In Singapore, a programme paid for by the government, AI Singapore, builds models called SEA-LION. Its first models were trained from scratch. Later ones took open models made by other companies and taught them more languages of the region. A 2025 paper by its team says they support 11 languages, such as Burmese, Khmer, Lao, Tamil and Thai. With partners in Thailand and the Philippines, the team also collects writing and speech in the region's languages. But to cover a language is not the same as to work well in it. The paper's main tests covered only four languages. In November 2024, two companies in Jakarta launched Sahabat-AI. It was made for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese. Its makers said it was at an early stage. In 2025, they added Balinese and Batak, working with universities and news groups. Speakers can help a tool fit their community, but people still need to test it.
read.sections.2.text.back: In Singapore there is a government-funded project called AI Singapore, which built a model called SEA-LION. The first version was trained new from the start; later versions took open models other companies had built and taught them more about the region's languages. The team's 2025 report says the model supports 11 languages, such as Burmese, Khmer, Lao, Tamil and Thai. The team also works with partners in Thailand and the Philippines to collect writing and speech in the region's languages. But supporting a language does not mean working well in it: the report's main test covered only four languages. In November 2024 two companies in Jakarta launched Sahabat-AI, built for Indonesian, Javanese and Sundanese. Its makers say the tool is still at an early stage. In 2025 they added Balinese and Batak, working with universities and news media groups. Speakers of a language help make a tool fit their community, but people still need to test the tool.
read.sections.2.text.note: Burmese as ภาษาพม่า (KEY_TERMS has Myanmar = เมียนมา for the country only); Sundanese as ภาษาซุนดา, Batak as ภาษาบาตัก. "support" a language = รองรับ. Avoided เท่านั้น throughout: the checker's ท่าน rule matches inside it.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: In Singapore, a team called AI Singapore makes SEA-LION. A 2025 report says it covers 11 languages of the region. The team also collects writing and speech in them. But to cover a language does not mean to work well in it. The team's main tests used only four of the 11. In 2024, two firms in Jakarta made Sahabat-AI. It was for Indonesian and two more languages. Its makers said it was still new. Speakers can help a tool fit their community. But people must still test it.

watch.summary.source: This video asks why AI tools work better in some languages than in others. A tool like a chatbot learns by reading lots of writing. The video says it is like a giant bookshop. But the bookshop has a problem. Most of its books are in English and a few other big languages. Languages with little writing online are called low-resource languages. The tools know much less about them. The video looks at two of these, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. It also shows researchers who built an open model in many languages, with help from local communities. The presenter says a few big companies decide what goes into these tools. He says it matters to everyone that AI tools include many languages.
watch.summary.back: This video asks why AI tools work better in some languages than others. Tools like chatbots learn by reading lots of writing. The video says it is like a giant bookshop, but this bookshop has a problem: most books are in English and a few other big languages. Languages with little writing on the internet are called low-resource languages, and tools know them much less. The video gives two examples, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. It also shows researchers building open models in many languages with help from local communities. The presenter says a few big companies decide what goes into these tools. He says it matters for everyone that AI tools include many languages.

educatorNotes.0.source: Harbourside and its three languages are made up. The real facts, with their scope: Stanford HAI (2025, Sanmi Koyejo's policy paper) defines low-resource languages as those with limited computer-readable data and gives Swahili (about 200 million speakers) as an example; it reports that major models serve English well, Vietnamese (97 million speakers) less well and Nahuatl (1.5 million) worse, and that translation “is unlikely to solve the problem”. “Low-resource” is about data for a task, never a language's worth, and a language can be low-resource for one task and not another. Less data is one possible cause of a gap, not a full diagnosis: how a model is built, tuned and tested matters too (Lesson 8). Schooling: UNESCO's Languages Matter (21 February 2025) says 40% of people lack education in their first or most fluent language, rising to 90% in some low- and middle-income countries; the lesson's link from schools, publishing, government and online use to the writing available is an explanation, not a measured result. Masakhane's own description says the colonial past was “devastating for African languages” in technology; it is presented as their view.
educatorNotes.0.back: Harbourside and its three languages are fictional. The facts and their scope: Stanford HAI (2025, a policy brief by Sanmi Koyejo) defines low-resource languages as languages with limited computer-readable data and gives Swahili (about 200 million speakers) as an example. The report says main models work well with English, less well with Vietnamese (97 million speakers) and worse with Nahuatl (1.5 million), and that translation is “unlikely to solve the problem”. “Low-resource” means data for a task, never the worth of a language, and a language can be low-resource for one task but not another. Less data is only one possible cause of the gap, not a full diagnosis; how models are built, tuned and tested matters too (Lesson 8). On education, UNESCO's Languages Matter (21 February 2025) says 40 percent of people do not get education in their first language or the language they know best, rising to 90 percent in some low- and middle-income countries. The link the lesson draws between schools, publishing, government and online use and the writing available is an explanation, not a measured result. Masakhane's own description says the colonial past “did serious damage to African languages” in technology; the lesson presents this as their view.
educatorNotes.0.note: Reviewer: UNESCO written ยูเนสโก, as in Lessons 11, 16 and 17.

educatorNotes.1.source: SEA-LION: the 2025 paper (arXiv 2504.05747, version 4, 30 October 2025) by AI Singapore (NUS) and NTU, funded by the National Research Foundation, describes Llama-SEA-LION-8B-IT and Gemma-SEA-LION-9B-IT; the family supports 11 languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, Thai, Burmese, Lao, Filipino, Tamil and Khmer). Its main benchmark (SEA-HELM) “only covers four languages”. AI Singapore's GitHub lists versions from v1 (3B and 7B, trained from scratch) to v4.8 (late 2026, built on NVIDIA Nemotron models, which it says covers 13 regional languages); versions change often, so the lesson gives only the paper's count. SEA-LION's own About page (sea-lion.ai/about) could not be opened through the approved route on 8 November 2026, so nothing in the lesson rests on it. SEALD (AI Singapore with Google Research, VISTEC in Thailand, and Ateneo and XFORM in the Philippines, from March 2024) collects text and speech in nine regional languages. Sahabat-AI: GoTo's release (15 November 2024) says it was co-developed with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, launched with 8- and 9-billion-parameter open models for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese, showed “leading performance” against similar open models (the makers' claim, with no published scores) and was “still in the early stage”; on 2 June 2025 a 70-billion-parameter version added Balinese and Batak, with six universities and four media groups. These are developers' descriptions, not independent tests. For the Jakarta pilot, Sahabat-AI's languages are a local link, but learners never need to name a language they speak. Accept any supported view of what these projects still need. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW07.md.
educatorNotes.1.back: SEA-LION: the 2025 report (arXiv 2504.05747 version 4, 30 October 2025) by AI Singapore (NUS) and NTU, funded by the National Research Foundation, describes Llama-SEA-LION-8B-IT and Gemma-SEA-LION-9B-IT. The family supports 11 languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, Thai, Burmese, Lao, Filipino, Tamil and Khmer). The main benchmark (SEA-HELM) “covers only four languages”. AI Singapore's GitHub lists versions from v1 (3B and 7B trained from scratch) to v4.8 (late 2026, built on an NVIDIA Nemotron model said to cover 13 languages of the region). Versions change often, so the lesson gives only the count in the report. SEALD (AI Singapore with Google Research and VISTEC in Thailand, and Ateneo and XFORM in the Philippines, from March 2024) collects text and speech in nine languages of the region. Sahabat-AI: GoTo's press release (15 November 2024) says it was developed with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, launched with open models of 8 and 9 billion parameters for Indonesian, Javanese and Sundanese, showed “leading performance” against similar open models (the makers' claim, no published scores) and is “still in its early stages”. On 2 June 2025 a 70-billion-parameter version added Balinese and Batak, with six universities and four media groups. All of this is the developers' description, not independent testing. For the Jakarta pilot, Sahabat-AI's languages are a local link, but learners never need to say what languages they speak. Accept any evidence-backed view of what these projects still need.
